title: Tail latency deep dive (Dedicated) - mixed prompt workloads
topics: Mixed prompt-length traffic (chat + long-context summarization) and p95/p99 latency spikes
Dedicated deployment expectations (SLOs, isolation, noisy neighbor)
Short/long prompt-aware scheduler prototype (two-queue policy, fairness bounds)
Instrumentation (prefill vs decode, queue wait time, queue depth, starvation signals)
Canary approach (feature flag, A/B, rollback criteria)
summary: HelioBank described tail latency spikes when interactive chat traffic is co-scheduled with long-context summarization jobs (10k–80k token contexts). Redwood walked through the mixed-workload scheduler prototype: classify prefill-heavy requests vs short/interactive requests, dispatch with short-first priority plus fairness window / starvation bounds, and separate backpressure under overload. Discussed success criteria (p95 improvement for short requests without >~5% throughput regression; no long-prompt starvation), required metrics, and a canary plan on Dedicated with the feature flag default-off and staged rollout/rollback triggers.
questions: Can the scheduler guarantee a max wait time bound for long prompts, or just probabilistic fairness?
Do you classify based on prompt tokens only, or predicted prefill cost (and does that adapt per model/hardware)?
How do you avoid short requests getting stuck behind a long prefill batch (priority inversion)?
What rollback triggers do you recommend for a Dedicated canary (queue depth, p99, error rate, GPU saturation)?
next_steps: HelioBank to share a 24h anonymized request histogram (prompt tokens, output tokens, concurrency) and their current p95/p99 SLO targets.
Redwood to propose a benchmark scenario mirroring HelioBank’s mix (interactive + long-context summarization bursts) and run it on A100 and H100 Dedicated SKUs.
Redwood to send a draft canary plan (feature flag enablement steps, dashboards to pin, rollback thresholds) for HelioBank review.
Schedule a 60-min follow-up to review benchmark output tables and decide whether to proceed with a Dedicated pilot slice.
action_items: Owner: Maya Chen (HelioBank) — Provide prompt-length and output-length distributions (p50/p95/p99) and peak QPS/concurrency by Friday.
Owner: Priya Nair (HelioBank) — Share current SLO docs (timeouts, p95/p99) and any recent incident notes tied to tail spikes.
Owner: Omar El-Sayed (Redwood) — Run mixed-workload replay benchmark with a long-context burst overlay; summarize p95 deltas and throughput impact.
Owner: Julian Moore (Redwood) — Send metric names / dashboard screenshots for per-class queue depth, wait time histograms, and starvation guardrails.
Owner: Lauren Bishop (Redwood) — Draft pilot/canary proposal for Dedicated (slice size, duration, approval checklist, rollback criteria).
transcript:
Meeting: Tail latency deep dive (Dedicated) - mixed prompt workloads
Recorded: 2024-11-05 17:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Lauren Bishop, Omar El-Sayed, Sofia Ivanova, Julian Moore
- HelioBank: Maya Chen, Eric Dalton, Priya Nair, Jonas Klein

---

[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is to go deep on the tail latency you’re seeing and how we’re thinking about mixed workloads on Dedicated. Omar and Sofia are here because they’ve been living in the scheduler prototype.

[00:18] Maya Chen: Yep, thanks. We’re basically trying to get chat to feel snappy while we also do these long-context summarization runs. And the moment summarization ramps, our chat p95 just… like it goes weird.

[00:32] Priya Nair: And p99 goes off a cliff. We see timeouts. It’s not constant, it’s like in windows when the long stuff starts.

[00:42] Omar El-Sayed: Got it. When you say long-context, what are we talking in tokens?

[00:46] Maya Chen: It varies. Typical summarization prompt is 10k to 30k. But some are 60k, and we have a few at 80k. Output is maybe 500 to 2k tokens.

[00:59] Eric Dalton: Chat is more like 200 to 800 tokens in, and maybe 100 to 400 out, streaming.

[01:07] Sofia Ivanova: So it’s very prefill-heavy on the summarization side and decode-heavy-ish on chat, with streaming. That’s the exact pattern that makes FIFO scheduling look bad.

[01:17] Jonas Klein: Right now we’re on vLLM self-hosted. We’ve tuned batching, but the tail is rough under mix. We’re evaluating Dedicated because we need predictable latency.

[01:28] Lauren Bishop: Makes sense. Also just to anchor: on Dedicated we can isolate capacity, but inside a given GPU pool you can still get contention between request shapes. The thing we’re prototyping is scheduler behavior that is explicitly prompt-length aware.

[01:44] Priya Nair: Is that like two queues?

[01:46] Sofia Ivanova: Yeah, two-queue is the simplest way to say it. Short/interactive queue and long/prefill-heavy queue. But with guardrails so the long queue doesn’t starve.

[02:00] Omar El-Sayed: Before we go there, can you describe the symptom in numbers? Like chat p95 baseline and then during summarization windows.

[02:09] Maya Chen: Sure. Chat p95 end-to-end is like 900ms when we’re just doing chat. During summarization, it’s 2.5s to 4s, depending on load. And p99 can be 8s, which is above our gateway timeout.

[02:25] Priya Nair: We basically have a 6s timeout on the edge. And we’re seeing 1-2% timeouts during those windows.

[02:33] Omar El-Sayed: And the long summarization requests, do you care about their latency? Or mostly throughput / finishing eventually.

[02:40] Maya Chen: They can be slower. Like, it’s okay if summarization takes 30 seconds. It’s not okay if chat takes 4 seconds.

[02:47] Sofia Ivanova: Great, that’s the policy lever. We can prioritize latency-sensitive without fully killing throughput.

[02:54] Julian Moore: One question: are these summarization requests arriving in bursts? Like a job kicks off and submits a bunch.

[03:00] Eric Dalton: Exactly. Batch job runs every 15 minutes. It can fire like 200 requests over a couple minutes.

[03:07] Julian Moore: Okay, that’s the classic burst pattern that creates queue depth and priority inversion.

[03:13] Lauren Bishop: Cool. So, what we’re building: a mixed-workload scheduler prototype in the runtime. It’s behind a feature flag, default off. The idea is to classify requests into short vs long based on expected prefill cost.

[03:29] Maya Chen: Based on token count?

[03:31] Sofia Ivanova: Initially yes, prompt tokens as a proxy. But we’re also adding a predicted prefill cost hook, because prompt tokens don’t map 1:1 across models and quantization, and some prompts have different attention patterns. We do a conservative default threshold and we can refine.

[03:49] Omar El-Sayed: And importantly we measure prefill vs decode time explicitly, so we can see whether the classification is wrong. Like if something got labeled short but actually spent forever in prefill.

[04:02] Priya Nair: What’s the actual scheduling policy, like strict priority?

[04:06] Sofia Ivanova: Not strict. Strict priority makes starvation likely for long. It’s “short-first with fairness window” is the internal name. Practically: we service short queue aggressively, but we guarantee long queue gets served at least every N dispatches or within a max wait bound.

[04:23] Jonas Klein: So something like weighted fair queueing?

[04:26] Sofia Ivanova: Similar spirit. Two-queue WFQ-ish, but tuned for GPU batch formation realities. Like, we can’t always interleave arbitrarily without breaking batching efficiency, so we do it in a stable pattern.

[04:39] Omar El-Sayed: And we added guardrail metrics: long-queue max wait time, long-queue age percentiles, and also short-queue backlog. If fairness is failing, you’ll see it quickly.

[04:50] Maya Chen: The biggest thing for us is: how do you stop short requests getting stuck behind a long prefill batch. That’s what I suspect we have today.

[05:00] Sofia Ivanova: Yeah, priority inversion. So there are two parts. One is queueing: don’t let long prefill requests occupy the only dispatch lane when short are waiting. The second is how the runtime forms batches. We discovered an edge case where a long prefill batch held the scheduling lock long enough that short requests couldn’t be dispatched. We fixed that in our internal branch. It’s basically ensuring we can preempt at the scheduler decision boundary.

[05:22] Julian Moore: Not preempt mid-kernel, to be clear. GPUs don’t love that. It’s more: you don’t keep feeding the long batch if the short queue is non-empty and you’re outside the fairness constraints.

[05:36] Priya Nair: So no kernel-level preemption.

[05:38] Sofia Ivanova: Correct, no kernel preemption. This is queue + dispatch policy.

[05:45] Lauren Bishop: From a product perspective, for Dedicated, we’d roll this out as an opt-in flag. For your pilot, we can do A/B in the same environment and compare.

[05:58] Jonas Klein: Compare how? Like same traffic mirrored?

[06:01] Omar El-Sayed: There are a few options. In our perf-canary we do a controlled replay. For a customer pilot, we can either (a) replay representative traces, or (b) split traffic by a deterministic hash so baseline and flag-on see similar mixes. If you can’t split due to stateful chat sessions, we can do a time-sliced canary with careful comparison, but split is better.

[06:24] Maya Chen: We can probably split by user_id hash. That’s fine.

[06:29] Priya Nair: What metrics are you looking at? We care about end-to-end, but I want to know what you’re measuring inside.

[06:36] Julian Moore: We instrument a few layers:
- Queue depth per class (short/long)
- Queue wait time histograms per class
- Service time split: prefill time vs decode time
- Scheduler decision trace spans (enqueue, dequeue, dispatch reason)
- Starvation signal: max wait time and “oldest request age”

[06:57] Omar El-Sayed: And then we correlate with GPU saturation metrics. Because sometimes p95 is just saturation, but often it’s scheduling ordering.

[07:06] Priya Nair: Do you have a recommended rollback criteria? Like what would page our on-call.

[07:11] Lauren Bishop: We typically do: if chat p95 regresses by more than X% for more than Y minutes, rollback. Also if error rate or timeouts go up. But for this feature specifically, SRE asked us to add: if long-queue max wait exceeds a bound for sustained time, that’s also a rollback because it means fairness broke.

[07:31] Sofia Ivanova: There’s also a “backlog growth” trigger. If queue depth is monotonically increasing, you’re unstable under that load.

[07:39] Maya Chen: Can you share what the success metrics look like for you? Like what do you consider a win.

[07:45] Omar El-Sayed: For the prototype we’ve been using targets like: under a mixed distribution (say 80% short, 20% long with long prompt lengths), improve short p95 by 20-40% vs FIFO. Keep throughput regression under ~5% in steady state. And enforce no long starvation: long max wait bounded, like under a few seconds to start service depending on configured knobs.

[08:09] Jonas Klein: But our long requests are like, huge. Is the max wait realistic?

[08:13] Sofia Ivanova: The bound is “time to first service / dispatch,” not time to completion. For long prompts, completion could be tens of seconds, but we ensure they keep making progress and aren’t blocked indefinitely.

[08:27] Eric Dalton: That’s fine. Our batch jobs can tolerate longer makespan.

[08:33] Maya Chen: What about streaming. Does streaming requests count as short by default?

[08:38] Sofia Ivanova: Not automatically. Streaming tends to be interactive, but it can also be long prompts. We don’t want to use streaming as the only signal. We can incorporate route hints or customer tier hints, but the safe default is prompt length / predicted prefill.

[08:55] Omar El-Sayed: Also, streaming is mostly about decode cadence. The pain you described is prefill contention, because long prompts dominate attention compute upfront.

[09:05] Priya Nair: Is there any chance the scheduler hurts batching efficiency and increases cost a lot.

[09:10] Omar El-Sayed: That’s the main tradeoff. Short-first can reduce batch size for long requests, which can lower throughput. That’s why we cap it with weights and fairness windows. We also measure “tokens/sec” and “GPU duty cycle.” If cost spikes, we’ll see it.

[09:28] Sofia Ivanova: And there’s a stability angle: under bursty long traffic, if you over-prioritize short, you can build an unbounded long backlog, which later causes a cliff. So we explicitly design to be stable: drain some long even when shorts keep arriving.

[09:47] Jonas Klein: How do you pick the thresholds for short vs long? Because our prompt distribution is bimodal.

[09:54] Sofia Ivanova: We start with a token threshold that’s conservative. Then we can tune based on observed prefill time. We’re experimenting with a rolling EWMA of prefill time to adjust the cutoff per model and hardware. But we’re cautious: you don’t want it to oscillate.

[10:14] Julian Moore: We also log sampled classification decisions. Like: prompt_tokens, predicted_cost_bucket, class=short/long, and then the observed prefill_ms. That helps debug mislabeling.

[10:29] Maya Chen: If we do a pilot, do we get access to those logs?

[10:33] Lauren Bishop: We can expose aggregated dashboards in the Console and share sampled logs via support channel, depending on your logging integration. On Dedicated, we can also route logs to your sink if configured.

[10:47] Priya Nair: Security-wise, we’d want logs in our Splunk. But we can handle later.

[10:53] Lauren Bishop: Yup.

[11:00] Omar El-Sayed: Can I ask: do you currently run chat and summarization on the same model? Or different models.

[11:05] Maya Chen: Same base model right now, different prompts. We might split later but for now it’s the same.

[11:12] Omar El-Sayed: That’s good for this. If it’s different models, you might also want routing separation.

[11:18] Jonas Klein: We tried separate deployments but it’s expensive. We want one pool if possible.

[11:24] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly why we’re doing this. Mixed workload in one pool.

[11:30] Eric Dalton: How does Dedicated isolation work if another customer is noisy.

[11:34] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated is physically allocated GPU capacity to you (reserved pool). So other customers won’t share those GPUs. The “noisy neighbor” you’re seeing today is internal: your own long jobs affecting your own chat.

[11:49] Priya Nair: Right.

[11:51] Maya Chen: Okay, can we talk about what a canary looks like in practice?

[11:55] Lauren Bishop: Sure. We’d keep default behavior as baseline. Then we enable “mixed_workload_scheduler” flag for, say, 5% of traffic on one route. We pin dashboards: chat p50/p95/p99, summarization throughput, queue depths, max wait. We set rollback triggers. We run for 24-48 hours to capture your batch job cycles.

[12:21] Omar El-Sayed: And we do A/B comparison snapshots around the burst windows. Like align on the same time-of-day jobs.

[12:29] Priya Nair: If it goes bad, how fast can you roll back.

[12:33] Lauren Bishop: Immediate. It’s a config toggle. No deploy needed.

[12:38] Julian Moore: From the runtime perspective, it’s a hot flag read. Worst case a few seconds to propagate.

[12:45] Jonas Klein: Are there any risks where turning it on causes instability.

[12:49] Sofia Ivanova: The main risks we’ve tracked: misclassification (long treated as short) which can break your short queue; oscillation if thresholds adapt too aggressively; and starvation if fairness window is mis-set. That’s why we ship with conservative defaults and alerts.

[13:11] Omar El-Sayed: Also backpressure. Under overload, if you accept infinite long requests, you’ll drown and eventually short suffers anyway. We’re separating admission control thresholds by class so long bursts don’t inflate the short queue latency.

[13:28] Priya Nair: That’s interesting. So you might reject long jobs earlier.

[13:32] Omar El-Sayed: Or queue them upstream, yes. Depends on how you want it. Some customers prefer 429s on batch routes rather than killing chat.

[13:43] Maya Chen: For batch we can handle retries. For chat we prefer not to error.

[13:49] Lauren Bishop: We can align on that. Dedicated lets you set per-route policies.

[14:00] Eric Dalton: I’m curious: do you have benchmark numbers you can share? Like do you see p95 improvements with this.

[14:06] Omar El-Sayed: We have internal numbers on representative mixes. I can’t share the raw customer traces, but we can share the deltas. For example, in our synthetic “80/20 short/long” with long prompts at 16k tokens, we saw short p95 drop ~30% with around 2-4% throughput hit depending on hardware.

[14:27] Sofia Ivanova: And p99 improves more than p95 typically, because you’re removing the “short stuck behind long” tail.

[14:35] Maya Chen: That’s what we want.

[14:38] Jonas Klein: Our long prompts are bigger than 16k though.

[14:41] Omar El-Sayed: Right, which is why we want to run your distribution.

[14:46] Lauren Bishop: That’s a good segue: if you can provide a histogram of prompt sizes and concurrency, we can create a benchmark scenario in our harness.

[14:55] Priya Nair: We can share an anonymized histogram and request timings.

[15:00] Maya Chen: We have logs with prompt tokens and output tokens. We can strip content.

[15:05] Omar El-Sayed: Perfect. That’s all we need.

[15:10] (crosstalk)

[15:11] Eric Dalton: One more question: we use Bedrock for some workloads. Their latency is stable-ish but expensive. If we move chat to Dedicated, we need to know p95 is stable.

[15:24] Lauren Bishop: Understood. And to be candid: no system can promise absolute p95 under arbitrary bursts if you’re saturating GPUs. But the goal is: for the same capacity and same load, remove the avoidable tail from poor scheduling.

[15:40] Priya Nair: So we still need to size capacity.

[15:42] Lauren Bishop: Exactly.

[15:46] Sofia Ivanova: And we can also use quotas / rate limits on the batch route to prevent it from consuming the whole pool.

[15:55] Maya Chen: Today our batch job just floods. We can throttle.

[16:00] Omar El-Sayed: If you throttle upstream plus scheduler improvements, you’ll get much better tail.

[16:07] Jonas Klein: Where does Triton fit in? We looked at Triton with custom scheduling.

[16:13] Omar El-Sayed: Triton’s great for classic DL serving, but LLM inference has these unique prefill/decode phases and continuous batching. You can build it, but Redwood’s runtime is purpose-built for that and we’re investing in this mixed phase-aware scheduling.

[16:30] Maya Chen: Got it.

[16:32] Julian Moore: Maybe helpful: we separate metrics by prefill and decode so you can see whether p95 is queue wait vs service. Often the “tail” is 80% waiting.

[16:43] Priya Nair: That aligns with what we see. GPU is pegged and queue grows.

[16:49] Sofia Ivanova: Pegged GPU isn’t automatically bad; it’s expected. What matters is: are you spending that GPU time on the right mix.

[16:58] Lauren Bishop: We’re at ~17 minutes. I want to make sure we cover your success criteria. What would make you say yes to Dedicated with this feature.

[17:07] Maya Chen: For chat: p95 under 1.2 seconds during summarization windows. And p99 under 4 seconds ideally. With <0.2% timeouts.

[17:18] Priya Nair: And for batch, I just want it to finish within like 45 minutes for the full run.

[17:24] Jonas Klein: Also, we need to see that enabling this doesn’t reduce overall tokens/sec massively.

[17:31] Omar El-Sayed: That’s consistent. We’ll propose a benchmark and share p95/p99 and throughput deltas.

[17:39] Sofia Ivanova: We’ll also define fairness: long queue max wait and progress rate. We can tune the weights.

[17:47] Eric Dalton: We might need to ensure specific tenants are prioritized. Like VIP chat.

[17:52] Lauren Bishop: That’s possible with routing policy / tiers. But for the prototype we’re focusing on short vs long. Tier-aware scheduling is a later extension.

[18:06] Maya Chen: Okay.

[18:08] (brief audio glitch)

[18:12] Julian Moore: Sorry, I missed a word. Did you say VIP chat by tenant.

[18:16] Eric Dalton: Yeah, but not required for POC.

[18:19] Julian Moore: Cool.

[18:22] Omar El-Sayed: One more technical detail: your 80k prompts — are those within one request, or chunked.

[18:29] Maya Chen: One request. We’re using a long-context model.

[18:33] Omar El-Sayed: Okay. Then prefill is huge. The scheduler will help, but you’ll likely also want to cap max concurrency for those, because two 80k prefills in parallel can dominate.

[18:48] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly. Part of backpressure by class: limit how many long-prefill requests can be in-flight.

[18:56] Priya Nair: That’s basically what we want.

[19:00] Lauren Bishop: Let’s talk next steps. We’ll send you a short list of data we need for the benchmark. Then we’ll draft a canary plan and dashboard checklist.

[19:12] Maya Chen: Works.

[19:13] Jonas Klein: Can you also clarify timeline? When is this actually available.

[19:18] Lauren Bishop: The scheduler is prototype behind a flag in the upcoming runtime release line (internally we call it 1.19). For a pilot we can enable it in your Dedicated environment before it’s generally available, but it stays default-off.

[19:36] Priya Nair: We’d want it default-off and we turn on.

[19:39] Lauren Bishop: Exactly.

[19:41] Omar El-Sayed: And we’ll be explicit about rollback: if chat p95 regresses, flip it off.

[19:49] Maya Chen: Great.

[19:51] (pause)

[19:54] Lauren Bishop: Any other questions before we wrap?

[19:58] Eric Dalton: Maybe just: if we do this and it works, does it become the default later.

[20:04] Sofia Ivanova: If the data supports it, we’ll likely graduate it to default-on for some routes or tiers, but only after more canary evidence. For now it’s a gated option.

[20:16] Jonas Klein: Makes sense.

[20:18] Priya Nair: Cool. Thanks.

[20:21] Lauren Bishop: Alright. We’ll follow up with the action items. Appreciate it.

---
